emberserve__36f4e93-0.vague: The HTTP load generator reports streaming requests as successful even when the server emitted an error event mid-stream or the connection dropped before the response finished. Those requests should show up as failures, with a reason, not as completed requests.
emberserve__36f4e93-0.precise: In the benchmark harness's HTTP client (pagedserve/bench/load.py, `_one_request`, reached through `run_http_benchmark`), a streaming request against /v1/chat/completions or /v1/completions is recorded as a success as soon as at least one token chunk arrived, regardless of how the stream ended. Two cases are wrong. (1) If the server returns HTTP 200 and then sends an SSE event whose JSON has a top-level `error` object (e.g. `{"error": {"message": "engine died", "type": "server_error"}}`) after some tokens, the event is silently skipped because it carries no `choices`, and the request ends up `success=True`. Expected: `success=False` with `error` containing the server's message text ("engine died" in that example), and the failed record should carry the wall-clock time (perf_counter seconds) at which the request gave up in a field named `end_s`, so the run's duration can include failed requests; today a failed record has no such timestamp. (2) If the stream ends (the body closes) after token chunks but without a `[DONE]` sentinel and without any choice carrying a non-null `finish_reason`, the request is still a success. Expected: `success=False` with an `error` string that says the stream ended before completion (containing the words "before completion"). A stream that ends with `[DONE]` or with a chunk whose choice has a `finish_reason` remains a success. Reproduce with an httpx.MockTransport that streams `data: <json>\n\n` lines and pass it as `transport=` to `run_http_benchmark`.

emberserve__36f4e93-1.vague: Benchmark summaries overstate throughput when some requests fail: a run where failed requests kept timing out after the last successful one reports a shorter duration than the wall time the load generator actually spent, so tokens/s comes out too high.
emberserve__36f4e93-1.precise: `summarize()` in pagedserve/bench/metrics.py computes the run's default duration (when `wall_s` is not passed) as the latest `finish_s` among successful records minus the earliest `arrival_s` over all records. Failed records never contribute, so a failure that gave up after the last success is dropped from the duration and `throughput_tok_s` is inflated (a real run: 46.04 s of duration out of 61.37 s wall, 141 tok/s reported vs ~106 actual). Expected: a failed record should be able to carry the time at which it gave up in a `RequestRecord` field named `end_s` (float seconds on the same clock as `arrival_s`/`finish_s`, default None), and `summarize()` should take the duration as the later of the last successful `finish_s` and the last failed record's `end_s`, minus the first arrival. Concretely, for a successful record arriving at 0.0 and finishing at 10.0 with 100 output tokens plus a failed record (`success=False`, `finish_s=None`) arriving at 1.0 with `end_s=20.0`, the summary should report `duration_s == 20.0`, `throughput_tok_s == 5.0` (only successful tokens count as output) and `completed == 1`.

emberserve__36f4e93-2.vague: In the offline benchmark, requests that queue behind an earlier static batch report latency that leaves out their queue wait, so static batching looks better than it is. Three requests that all arrive at t=0 end up with three different arrival timestamps in the results.

With `static_batching=True` and `max_num_seqs=1`, a trace of three requests all with `arrival_s=0.0` is admitted one at a time as each batch drains, so the three records get three distinct `arrival_s` values and their `ttft_s` excludes the time spent waiting for the previous batch. Expected: all three records share one `arrival_s` (the offer time), and their TTFTs strictly increase in admission order because the queued requests waited. The same offset applies to continuous batching, where a request waits for the running step before admission.

emberserve__36f4e93-4.vague: When benchmarking a chat-completions endpoint, time-to-first-token comes out near zero and the output token count is two too high: the harness is treating the initial role announcement chunk and the final finish chunk as tokens.

emberserve__4e0b5f0-0.vague: Step traces are wrong for requests that use a repetition penalty under async scheduling: every step shows zero host resolve time even when resolving the step took tens of milliseconds, and the GPU gap after the engine drains is attributed to host lag.

Currently the records show `host_resolve_ms` of 0 and `idle()` is never called on this path.

emberserve__4e0b5f0-1.vague: Benchmarking pagedserve's own /v1/completions endpoint with a one-token completion gets recorded as a failed "empty stream" request, because the server sends that single token with an empty text and the finish reason in the same chunk and the harness does not count it.

emberserve__4e0b5f0-2.vague: Benchmarks against vLLM report an inflated time-per-output-token: vLLM's completions stream ends with a separate usage-only chunk that arrives well after the last token, and the harness treats that trailer as if it were the last token.

emberserve__7edbe0f-2.vague: Under load with streaming clients, the API server can freeze completely: no responses come out and new requests hang, while the engine-core subprocess is still alive. It happens when a client stops reading and the engine's output pipe fills up.
emberserve__7edbe0f-2.precise: EngineCoreProcess.send() in pagedserve/server/engine_core.py writes commands directly into the command pipe on the caller's thread under a lock. The core process only reads commands between steps, so when it blocks writing a step's outputs into a full output pipe, the output reader thread on the API side (the only thing draining that pipe) blocks the moment it tries to send a stop-string abort, and the event loop blocks holding the send lock midway through a large `add`; nothing drains anything and the server deadlocks. Expected: sending a command to the core must never block the caller, even when nobody is reading the pipe and the payload is far larger than the pipe buffer (e.g. a 4 MiB add followed by two aborts returns in well under 0.5 s), and the messages must arrive in the order they were submitted. When the receiving end of the pipe has been closed, the first write fails asynchronously; the failure must be exposed on the writer as an `error` attribute (the caught exception, None until then), and any subsequent submission must raise BrokenPipeError. The hidden test exercises this through a helper class `_CommandWriter(conn)` in pagedserve.server.engine_core that takes a multiprocessing Connection, with `put(msg)`, an `error` attribute and `close()`; EngineCoreProcess.send should go through it.

emberserve__7edbe0f-3.vague: The Triton paged-attention decode kernel breaks for KV block sizes that are multiples of 16 but not powers of two: block size 48 errors out in the dot variant, and block size 96 reads the wrong keys for positions past 64, so attention output is wrong once a context grows beyond that.

For the dot variant the tile is `min(block_size, 64)`, and _tile_for() rounds a tile down to a power of two then takes `min(block_size, tile)`. The engine accepts any block_size that is a multiple of 16, so with block_size=48 the dot variant gets a 48-position tile, which is not a power of two and `tl.arange` rejects it (the kernel fails to compile/launch); with block_size=96 it gets a 64-position tile that does not divide the page, so positions 64..95 of each block are read from the next physical block and the result is wrong. The tile chosen must always be a power of two that divides block_size (16 always qualifies).
